report.source_text: On the day of the procedure, the patient was placed in the supine position. The right groin was prepped in a sterile fashion, and lidocaine was used as a local anesthetic. The procedure was begun using real-time ultrasound guidance with a micro-puncture needle to gain access to the right femoral artery. Following initial access, a 5-French vascular sheath was inserted. A catheter was placed over the wire and used to select the left common iliac artery, where further angiography was performed. This allowed the physician to identify the uterine artery, after which the microcatheter was advanced into it. A further angiogram of the uterine artery was performed and revealed a normal appearance of the uterus and fallopian tube with no evidence of arterial venous malformation or fistula. The interventional radiologist then performed angiography from the right uterine artery, which also demonstrated a normal appearance without evidence of AVM. At this point, the case was reviewed with another interventional radiologist who agreed, based on the angiographic images, that the uterine arteries were normal and without evidence of AVM (Figures 3-4).

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 24-year-old female presented to the ED with sudden-onset heavy vaginal bleeding and abdominal cramping approximately 4 hours prior to presentation. She had a history of miscarriage 2 months prior requiring D&C for retained products of conception and was amenorrheic on medroxyprogesterone at the time of presentation. Physical examination revealed remnants of bleeding at the external cervical os without active external bleeding or adnexal tenderness. Transvaginal ultrasound on admission demonstrated vibrant abnormal flow on color Doppler concerning for an AVM. Subsequently, angiography was performed and revealed normal bilateral uterine arteries with no evidence of AVM, findings confirmed by a second interventional radiologist. Approximately two weeks after initial presentation, pelvic MRI showed pathological abnormal endometrial enhancement. The patient reported two additional episodes of spontaneous, self-resolving heavy vaginal bleeding at the two-week follow-up. Follow-up after angiography revealed no further episodes of abnormal vaginal bleeding. The absence of AVM on angiography despite initial TVUS findings concerning for AVM, combined with the clinical course of self-resolving bleeding episodes, supports the diagnosis of spontaneously resolved AVM.

final.final_diagnosis: Spontaneously resolved arteriovenous malformation (AVM) of the uterus
final.trajectory_summary: A 24-year-old female presented to the ED with sudden-onset heavy vaginal bleeding and abdominal cramping approximately 4 hours prior to presentation. She had a history of miscarriage 2 months prior requiring D&C for retained products of conception and was amenorrheic on medroxyprogesterone at the time of presentation. Physical examination revealed remnants of bleeding at the external cervical os without active external bleeding or adnexal tenderness. Transvaginal ultrasound on admission demonstrated vibrant abnormal flow on color Doppler concerning for an AVM. Subsequently, angiography was performed and revealed normal bilateral uterine arteries with no evidence of AVM, findings confirmed by a second interventional radiologist. Approximately two weeks after initial presentation, pelvic MRI showed pathological abnormal endometrial enhancement. The patient reported two additional episodes of spontaneous, self-resolving heavy vaginal bleeding at the two-week follow-up. Follow-up after angiography revealed no further episodes of abnormal vaginal bleeding. The absence of AVM on angiography despite initial TVUS findings concerning for AVM, combined with the clinical course of self-resolving bleeding episodes, supports the diagnosis of spontaneously resolved AVM.
